title: Bohr's Dog Blood: Shifting the Curve

scenes.visual: Title card 'Bohr's Dog Blood: Shifting the Curve' over a glass flask of dark red blood. Reuses the first film's COLOUR MAP (both films): axes saturation (%) up, PO2 (mmHg) across; adult human curve RED; right-shifted curve ORANGE; one-site carriers TEAL (loose grip dashed, tight grip solid); lung band BLUE at about 100 mmHg; venous-blood band GREY at about 40 mmHg after resting tissue, sliding toward 20 mmHg after hard-working tissue (blood PO2 points, not tissue PO2); release drawn as a vertical GOLD bracket between the lung point and the tissue point; capacity tank RED outline. All curves are computed from the Severinghaus model of standard human blood (P50 26.8 mmHg) or from one-site formulas; every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: Working tissue pours out carbon dioxide. Does that change how tightly blood holds oxygen, or does carbon dioxide just ride along?
scenes.visual: A working muscle cartoon puffs grey 'CO2' bubbles into a passing RED blood vessel. Two labelled arrows from the bubbles: 'changes oxygen binding?' and 'just rides along?'
scenes.narration: Working tissue pours out carbon dioxide. Does that change how tightly blood holds oxygen, or does carbon dioxide just ride along?

scenes.tts: The first film showed blood delivering its drop in saturation, from lung to tissue. Now ask what makes that drop bigger where tissue is working.
scenes.visual: Brief replay of the first film's frame: RED S-curve, BLUE lung band, GREY venous-blood band at 40, GOLD bracket between the dots. A '?' appears over the bracket.
scenes.narration: The first film showed blood delivering its drop in saturation, from lung to tissue. Now ask what makes that drop bigger where tissue is working.

scenes.tts: In Copenhagen in nineteen oh three, Christian Bohr worked with Karl Hasselbalch and August Krogh. They took fresh dog blood.
scenes.caption: In Copenhagen in 1903, Christian Bohr worked with Karl Hasselbalch and August Krogh. They took fresh dog blood.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Copenhagen, 1903'. Three name cards: 'Christian Bohr', 'Karl Hasselbalch', 'August Krogh'. A flask of dark red blood labelled 'fresh dog blood'.
scenes.narration: In Copenhagen in 1903, Christian Bohr worked with Karl Hasselbalch and August Krogh. They took fresh dog blood.

scenes.tts: They exposed samples to gas at a set oxygen pressure, and measured how much oxygen the blood bound. Repeating this at many pressures traces the curve.
scenes.visual: A sealed flask (tonometer) rocks gently; a gas line feeds it, gauge 'PO2 set'. A reading drops one RED dot onto an empty saturation-PO2 frame. The flask repeats at other gauge settings; RED dots build up the S-curve (schematic points on the computed curve).
scenes.narration: They exposed samples to gas at a set oxygen pressure, and measured how much oxygen the blood bound. Repeating this at many pressures traces the curve.

scenes.tts: Then they raised the carbon dioxide in the gas, and measured again at the same oxygen pressures. If carbon dioxide simply rode along, nothing should change. Only carbon dioxide changed, so any difference came from it, or from the acid it forms.
scenes.visual: A second gauge 'CO2' turns from low to high; grey CO2 bubbles enter the flask. A dashed outline shows where the new dots would land if nothing changed: exactly on the RED curve.
scenes.narration: Then they raised the carbon dioxide in the gas, and measured again at the same oxygen pressures. If carbon dioxide simply rode along, nothing should change. Only carbon dioxide changed, so any difference came from it, or from the acid it forms.

scenes.tts: If something does change, where will it show most? At a low oxygen pressure, or near full saturation?
scenes.visual: Two spots on the RED curve pulse: one low on the steep part (label 'low PO2'), one high on the flat top (label 'near full'). Question card.
scenes.narration: If something does change, where will it show most? At a low oxygen pressure, or near full saturation?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: More carbon dioxide lowered oxygen binding. The effect was large at low oxygen pressures and small near full saturation. The curve had moved to the right.
scenes.visual: New ORANGE dots land below the RED curve: far below it at low PO2, barely below at the top. An ORANGE curve draws through them, shifted right (computed, schematic shift by stretching the pressure axis). Vertical arrows show the gap: long at low PO2, tiny near the top.
scenes.narration: More carbon dioxide lowered oxygen binding. The effect was large at low oxygen pressures and small near full saturation. The curve had moved to the right.

scenes.tts: Today this is called the Bohr effect: a fall in oxygen affinity when pH falls or carbon dioxide rises.
scenes.caption: Today this is called the Bohr effect: a fall in oxygen affinity when pH falls or carbon dioxide rises.
scenes.visual: Label card 'Bohr effect = lower affinity when pH falls or CO2 rises'. Small icons: a pH meter dropping, a CO2 gauge rising, both pointing at the ORANGE curve.
scenes.narration: Today this is called the Bohr effect: a fall in oxygen affinity when pH falls or carbon dioxide rises.

scenes.tts: The shift raises P fifty, the oxygen pressure at which hemoglobin is half full. A higher P fifty means a looser grip.
scenes.caption: The shift raises P50, the oxygen pressure at which hemoglobin is half full. A higher P50 means a looser grip.
scenes.visual: A horizontal dashed line at 50% saturation meets the RED curve, drop line to '26.8'; it meets the ORANGE curve further right, drop line to '32' (model illustration). Label 'P50 rises: looser grip'.
scenes.narration: The shift raises P50, the oxygen pressure at which hemoglobin is half full. A higher P50 means a looser grip.

scenes.tts: Now bring back the bands. In the lungs, the shifted curve is still nearly full. Loading barely changes.
scenes.visual: BLUE lung band and GREY venous-blood band (40, blood leaving resting tissue) reappear. In the BLUE band the ORANGE dot sits just under the RED one: labels '97.7%' and '96.2%'. Small label: 'whole curve shifted, model illustration'.
scenes.narration: Now bring back the bands. In the lungs, the shifted curve is still nearly full. Loading barely changes.

scenes.tts: But at tissue pressure the shifted curve sits lower. So the release bracket grows, by about two-fifths at rest in this model.
scenes.visual: In the GREY band the ORANGE dot sits clearly below the RED one: '74.9%' and '64.6%'. Two GOLD brackets side by side as bars: RED-blood release '4.6 mL per dL', ORANGE-blood release '6.4 mL per dL'. Label 'released from hemoglobin, model illustration'.
scenes.narration: But at tissue pressure the shifted curve sits lower. So the release bracket grows, by about two-fifths at rest in this model.

scenes.tts: And that happens where it matters. Working tissue is high in carbon dioxide and low in oxygen, so blood gives up more exactly there.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the muscle cartoon: grey CO2 bubbles thick around the working fibres, label 'high CO2, low PO2'. The passing blood stays drawn in one colour; an inset beside it shows the ORANGE curve with its longer GOLD bracket in the low-PO2 band, and extra BLUE oxygen dots stream out into the fibres.
scenes.narration: And that happens where it matters. Working tissue is high in carbon dioxide and low in oxygen, so blood gives up more exactly there.

scenes.tts: Published in nineteen oh four, the paper offered a reason why blood gives up oxygen more readily in active tissue.
scenes.caption: Published in 1904, the paper offered a reason why blood gives up oxygen more readily in active tissue.
scenes.visual: A paper card '1904' (published version) slides over the muscle scene; a highlighted phrase 'gives up oxygen more readily in active tissue'. ORANGE and RED curves shown as a small inset.
scenes.narration: Published in 1904, the paper offered a reason why blood gives up oxygen more readily in active tissue.

scenes.tts: Two other changes also shift the curve right. Warmer tissue lowers affinity, and working muscle is warmer than resting muscle. So does more B P G, a small molecule made in red cells.
scenes.caption: Two other changes also shift the curve right. Warmer tissue lowers affinity, and working muscle is warmer than resting muscle. So does more BPG, a small molecule made in red cells.
scenes.visual: Two short cards slide in beside the ORANGE curve: a thermometer rising, label 'higher temperature'; a red cell drawn open, with extra small blocks labelled 'BPG' staying inside it and docking in the central cavity of hemoglobin blocks that have no oxygen, label 'more BPG inside red cells'. Each card nudges an ORANGE arrow to the right.
scenes.narration: Two other changes also shift the curve right. Warmer tissue lowers affinity, and working muscle is warmer than resting muscle. So does more BPG, a small molecule made in red cells.

scenes.tts: They are separate effects, each with its own cause. The name Bohr effect is kept for pH and carbon dioxide alone.
scenes.visual: Three labelled boxes in a row: 'Bohr effect: pH and CO2', 'temperature', 'BPG'. A line tries to merge all three under 'Bohr effect' and fades out; the three boxes stay separate.
scenes.narration: They are separate effects, each with its own cause. The name Bohr effect is kept for pH and carbon dioxide alone.

scenes.tts: So a modest right shift costs little in the lungs, where blood loads. It pays out in working tissue, where blood unloads and the need is greatest.
scenes.visual: Final frame: RED and ORANGE curves together, nearly touching in the BLUE band, clearly apart in the GREY band, with the longer GOLD bracket on the ORANGE curve.
scenes.narration: So a modest right shift costs little in the lungs, where blood loads. It pays out in working tissue, where blood unloads and the need is greatest.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. Take-home line: 'A modest right shift barely costs loading but raises release in tissue.'
